title: Local References Cannot Escape
goal: Understand why references cannot outlive the function that created their data.

source.attribution: adapted from Comprehensive Rust: Borrowing & Memory Management

sections.text: In garbage-collected languages, returning a reference to an object created inside a function keeps the object alive on the heap. In Rust, local variables live on the stack and are dropped when the function returns.

sections.caption: Borrowing local data fails because title is dropped at the closing brace.

sections.text: If you return a reference to `title`, that reference becomes dangling the instant `create_title` finishes. Rust detects this at compile time and stops you with error `E0515`.
To hand data to a caller, move the owned value out instead of lending it. Returning `String` transfers ownership without copying any heap memory.

sections.caption: Returning the owned String moves the heap pointer to the caller.

sections.text: The same rule applies when modifying struct fields through a mutable reference. You cannot move a field out directly, but you can replace it using helper functions like `std::mem::take`.

explanation: Understand why references cannot outlive the function that created their data.
